methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a retrospective single-center cohort of 363 patients with a clinically homogeneous population (PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy, no oncogenic drivers), with a reasonable analytical strategy including treating irTD as a time-varying covariate and conducting landmark analyses at 3 and 6 months to mitigate immortal-time bias (Section 2.4). Multivariable Cox regression with pre-specified covariate entry (p<0.10 threshold) is appropriate. However, no a priori sample-size or power calculation is reported, important baseline confounders are missing (corticosteroid exposure, autoimmune history, inflammatory/comorbidity burden, antibody status), molecular profiling was restricted to EGFR/ALK (potentially leaving residual driver-positive patients), and overall survival is immature. No multiplicity correction is described for the multiple landmark and subgroup comparisons, but effect sizes and 95% CIs are consistently reported.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a retrospective, single-center observational cohort using a hospital registry, corresponding to Oxford CEBM level 2b (individual cohort study), with limitations (single center, retrospective, incomplete baseline covariates) nudging toward 4. The clinical question — whether irTD can serve as an on-treatment biomarker of pembrolizumab benefit in PD-L1-high NSCLC — is clinically meaningful, and the magnitude of the PFS signal (HR 0.378 unadjusted; HR 0.490 and 0.587 at 3- and 6-month landmarks) is substantial. However, PFS is a surrogate endpoint, OS is not reported, no validation cohort is included, and the findings mostly confirm a growing but still non-practice-changing literature, so the translational path remains hypothesis-generating rather than directly actionable.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is the applicable standard for this retrospective observational cohort. The manuscript reports eligibility criteria, data sources, variable definitions (hypo/hyperthyroidism cutoffs, SITC early/late onset threshold, CTCAE grading), statistical methods (time-varying Cox, landmark analyses), ethics approval, and limitations in reasonable detail. However, there is no participant flow diagram, no protocol registration, no explicit prespecification of primary vs. secondary outcomes, no description of missing-data handling, and no reporting of adverse events beyond the thyroid-specific focus. There is no data-availability statement, no public deposit of the dataset, and no code sharing, so reproducibility is minimal.

novelty_literature.justification: The central finding — that irTD during PD-1 blockade is associated with improved PFS in NSCLC — has already been reported by several of the comparator studies the authors cite (Chilelli, Cai, Thuillier, Wu, Cerić), and the manuscript explicitly frames itself as confirming this prior signal. The incremental novelty is empirical/population: a reasonably large (n=363), uniformly first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy, PD-L1 ≥50%, driver-negative cohort with systematic 6-weekly thyroid monitoring, plus an early-vs-late timing analysis. No new mechanism, assay, or conceptual framework is introduced, and the early/late timing comparison, while useful, is narrow and underpowered. Overall this is incremental confirmation with modest population refinement.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable with a conventional IMRaD structure, informative tables cited in the text, and a comprehensive, well-referenced discussion that situates findings against prior NSCLC irTD literature. The abstract is quantitatively grounded and self-contained, though it awkwardly contains what appears to be two overlapping abstract versions (a lay-style paragraph followed by a structured scientific version) that should be reconciled. Some repetition occurs between results and discussion, acronyms (irTD, irAE, TPS) are introduced appropriately, and the limitations section is unusually thorough. Minor issues include inconsistent reporting (TPS >50% in the aim vs. ≥50% elsewhere) and some long sentences in the discussion.

key_strengths: Clinically homogeneous cohort of 363 PD-L1 ≥50%, driver-negative, first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy patients with systematic 6-weekly thyroid monitoring
Appropriate handling of immortal-time bias via time-varying Cox covariate and 3- and 6-month landmark analyses, with consistent HRs across approaches
Large and consistent effect size (landmark HRs 0.49 and 0.59; p<0.001) supporting irTD as an on-treatment prognostic signal
Thorough limitations section acknowledging residual confounding, missing autoantibody data, and single-center retrospective design
key_concerns: Incremental novelty — the irTD–PFS association has been reported in multiple prior NSCLC cohorts cited by the authors
Immature overall survival; PFS is the only time-to-event endpoint, limiting clinical weight
Missing key confounders (corticosteroids, autoimmune history, comorbidities, inflammatory markers) and no thyroid autoantibody testing
Molecular profiling limited to EGFR/ALK — rare drivers (ROS1, BRAF, MET, KRAS G12C, etc.) not excluded
No data-availability statement, no code sharing, no protocol registration or STROBE flow diagram
Duplicated/overlapping abstract paragraphs and minor inconsistency in PD-L1 threshold reporting (>50% vs. ≥50%)
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically competent retrospective cohort with appropriate bias mitigation but incremental scientific contribution and immature OS data; best fit is a tier-3 oncology journal with minor revisions to add a flow diagram, data-availability statement, and reconcile the abstract.
